full_judgment:
5. Same date, the application was heard. Two issues, namely, whether the plaint is liable to be rejected, and whether the plaintiff is entitled to an order of injunction as prayed for were framed by the Court. It appears that the issue as to the rejection of the plaint was taken up by the Court suo mota. By the impugned order the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the application for temporary injunction, and also rejected the plaint being of the view that the suit is barred by limitation, and that the suit premises belongs to the Government and no such suit is maintainable against the Government. 

 7. Mr Probir Halder, learned Advocate for opposite party Nos. 1, 2 and 5, took us through the written objection of defendant No.1, the Samity and defending the impugned order submits that it was stated in the written objection that the suit premises belongs to the Government and no suit under section 9 of the Act lies against the Government and the learned Subordinate Judge therefore did not commit any error in rejecting the plaint. He also submits that learned Subordinate Judge did not commit any error of procedure in rejecting the plaint while disposing the application for temporary injunction since the Court is empowered to reject the plaint suo mota when the suit appears to him not maintainable. In support, he cites a decision in the case of Md Shamsul Hoque Malia vs Md Latifur Rahman 1989 BLD 524. He then reads out paragraph No. 6 of the written objection wherein it is written that in Title Suit No. 93 of 1997 before the First Court of Assistant Judge at Dhaka on 12-5-1997 the plaintiff filed an affidavit claiming that he did not do any work in the project and before the expiry of the period he shifted his business elsewhere and submits that the learned Subordinate Judge did not commit any error in relying upon such objection in finding that the suit is barred by limitation since it was filed on 1-3-2000 long after six months from said 12-5-1997. He also submits that the suit is also barred under section 133 of the Co-operative Societies Ordinance, 1984 since, according to him, the cause of action for recovery of possession is a dispute within the meaning of section 86 of the Ordinance to be referred to the Registrar. 

 8. We shall see whether the learned Subordinate Judge acted within his jurisdiction and the law in rejecting the plaint while disposing an application for temporary injunction. As stated above, the plaint was rejected on two grounds, namely, that as the suit premises belongs to the Government and no suit under section 9 of the Act against the Government is maintainable, and secondly, that the suit is barred by limitation as it was not brought within six months of the dispossession. 

 13. No such affidavit appears to have been produced before the Court below. Nor the defendants could produce the affidavit before us. Moreover, even if such statement made in a separate proceeding is taken on its face value that does not say that the plaintiff admitted thereby to have vacated the possession of the suit premises on or before 12-5-1997. Even the learned Subordinate Judge could not record a positive finding that the plaintiff vacated the possession of the suit premises on or before that date before he found the suit barred by limitation. We find the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the suit is barred by limitation is based on total disregard of the above averments made in the plaint. Moreover, it is now well established principle of law for safe guidance that the question of limitation is always a mixed question of law and facts, which can only be decided on evidence to be adduced at the trial of a suit. The finding on limitation as arrived at by the learned Subordinate Judge being not based on the averments made in the plaint but on extraneous considerations therefore cannot justify rejecting the plaint.
